beats.say: On the laptop, this command scores three saved predictions. Open the same project in a fresh clone. Watch the files as the commit arrives. The script travels. The settings file stays on the laptop. Which missing file would explain a failed score?
Ask Git to include ignored paths in its status. Two exclamation marks flag dot env. It holds a private setting, and this scorer needs no key. List the paths in the commit. The script is there.

Run the script in the clone. The error names the evaluation fixture. Its file is missing. Exit one tells us the run failed. The message names the input. Before changing Git, check where the shell looked. The shell runs commands in your terminal. In each window, its current directory matches the repository root.

Start at the top of access-rag. P W D prints the current directory. A relative path starts there. An absolute path starts at the filesystem root. From here, eval slash access requests dot jsonl reaches the fixture. Move into scripts with C D. The same relative path now looks for eval inside scripts.
That alone could explain a missing file.

Quote the input variable. The shell then passes a name containing a space as one argument. If you need to change directories in a script, check that you got there before launching the next command. The guard on screen exits on failure. In our opening both shells were already at the project root.

So check what Git could have supplied. Init creates a local repository. Add selects file contents. Commit records them locally. A clone checks out the files recorded in a commit. Sharing that commit with a remote takes a separate push.

On the original machine, ask Git for its short status, including individual untracked files. The two question marks mean this file is untracked here. In the teammate’s clone, look up that exact path in the tree recorded at HEAD. The prompt comes back without a filename.
That commit omitted the fixture. Two question marks describe the original working directory. The empty tree lookup tells us what the teammate actually received.

Read it as one JSON object per line, with a request, an expected label, and a saved prediction. Track this small test input. It lets your teammate run the same comparison without a live model. Keep the real secret, the virtual environment and generated caches local.
An example environment file can carry the names a program expects.
We want a teammate to receive the test data. The real environment file, virtual environment and generated runs can stay untracked. The pattern at the top covers names beginning with dot env.
The negated example pattern makes an exception for the file that holds a variable name with its value left blank. The small evaluation fixture matches no ignore rule.
Try an already tracked placeholder. There’s a working copy, a selected copy, and an older commit that contains it. Add its name to the ignore file. Which of those copies did that pattern remove?

All three remain. The new rule leaves it in the index. Git remove cached removes that selection while preserving the working file. Commit the removal. This still leaves old history available. Rotate an exposed active credential if a real one entered that history.
A force add can also select an ignored path. Inspect what you’re about to share.

Zoom in on request one hundred two. The expected answer is blocked. Our saved prediction says escalated. Watch what moves when I stage the file. Git copies its current contents into the index. That’s the selection a plain commit will record.

Now change the working prediction to blocked. Look across at the selected copy. Git diff compares these two views. You can see the word you changed and the word it replaced. A second git add would select the edit too.

Leave that edit on the laptop. Git diff cached compares the index with the current commit. This fixture is new, so the selected difference includes the whole row. Which prediction will a teammate receive?

Make the commit. Escalated travels from the index. Your editor still says blocked. Run both files against the same three answers. The laptop gets all three right. The clone gets two. Which comparison would have warned us? The working diff showed the unstaged edit.

title: What does one more miss cost?

beats.say: Run the committed copy. The approved request matches, so mark one correct and one seen. On the next row, blocked and escalated disagree. Only the total grows. The restored request matches too. You can account for the whole score with those three comparisons.

The terminal rounds two thirds to zero point six six seven. The gate uses the counts. Three times correct must be at least twice total. Six equals six, so this run passes. Suppose the next request is another miss. Will the gate still open?

Look at the end of the downloaded fixture. It ends at a closing brace. Insert a newline there so the next object starts on its own line. Now append request one hundred four. Watch the mark for the required count.
This extra miss raises the right side to eight and leaves the left at six. The scorer returns failure. The earlier missing file also gave exit one. This time we have a score to explain.

title: What does the file actually contain?

beats.say: What qualifies as a row? The article’s scorer skips blank lines and reads one JSON object per remaining line. Require prompt, expected and prediction. All three must contain nonempty text. The empty array is legal JSON, but it fails this object contract.
A missing required field, a record the decoder rejects, or an empty dataset stops the run before it prints a score.

Look inside this prompt. A Unicode line separator sits between two words in the quoted string. The article’s splitlines can cut that prompt in two. For a strict JSON Lines reader, open the UTF-eight file with the newline set to line feed. Decode every physical line.
One line feed ends request one hundred one. Add a second line feed. Now line two is blank. It has no JSON value, so the reader reports line two and stops.

Try a different input. The extra cost field here holds NaN, which means not a number. Python accepts that bare constant by default. Reject those constants during decoding to enforce strict JSON, and report the line if decoding fails. Then check the required fields as before.

Compare these two stored labels. Python applies strip and then lower to each label. For this pair, ordinary spaces come off the ends and the capital letters become lowercase. Both sides now hold the word blocked. If the prediction changes to escalated, the words differ even after that cleanup.

Back to the original three requests. Here are the ends of the lines in the copy with a trailing newline. Each closing brace finishes an object. Each blue zero A is a newline byte. Remove only its final newline. How many newlines will word count find? How many requests can Python still read?

Two blue marks remain. Word count reports two. Follow the braces, though. Python still parses three JSON objects and keeps two matches. The last prediction is intact. Use a line count to inspect a file. Use the parser and the label comparison to decide the gate.

Your teammate can run the tracked repro script by its path. A shortcut in your shell stays on your machine. To check a commit automatically, track the hook source and its installer too. The installer places an executable copy in this checkout’s private hooks directory. Repeat that installation in each clone.

Start with the original three requests. Add the wrong fourth request on its own line in the working file and stage all four rows. Try to commit them. Git runs the installed hook. Its scorer opens the working file on disk. Which rows will it see?
Two matches in four rows. The scorer returns one. Git stops the commit. Look at the index. All four requests are still staged.
If a different hook already occupies that path, the installer stops too. Check for a configured hooks path and merge the checks deliberately. A teammate can keep the checks they already depend on.

title: Which copy did the hook read?

beats.say: The extra request is still in the index from that blocked commit. Remove the trial row only from the working copy. Before committing, look at both diffs. The working diff shows a deletion. The staged diff still shows the addition. Try the plain commit again.
Watch the hook read the working file. It finds two matches in three rows, and the local hook passes. Which file will the clean checkout get?

Git records the index. Follow that file into a clean checkout in continuous integration, or C I. Run the same check there. Request one hundred four came along. Two matches in four rows fall below two thirds. The hook read the three working rows. C I read the four rows in the commit.
Once the commit exists, use git show HEAD to see the change it recorded. There’s the extra row. A local hook can be skipped. Have C I run the tracked command on the commit your teammate will receive.

Suppose yesterday’s commit passed this check. Today’s fails with a score. Save the output and exit status before changing any files. Start Git bisect in a clean working tree. Mark a known passing commit good and the failing one bad. Now Git can check out a revision between them.
Run the same command in the middle. Commit three passes. Move the good end there. Commit five fails with the extra miss. Move the bad end back. Which revision is left to check?

Commit four passes. Good and bad sit side by side. Five introduced the extra wrong row. Inspect that commit’s diff, then use bisect reset to return to your branch. If a candidate can’t run the scorer because setup is broken, skip it. Calling a setup failure bad would answer a different question.

title: What does a zero count tell you?

beats.say: Over S S H, ask head for one line. The first request shows the fields you’ll find in this file. Now count the newlines. This copy has one at the end of each request, so word count prints three.

Search the fixture for the word denied. Grep prints zero on standard output. It read the file and found no matching line, so it returns status one. Change only the filename. The new path names a file that does not exist. What will grep write to each stream, and what status will it return?
The error names the missing file. On this Linux host, grep sends that message to standard error and returns status two. Its standard output is empty. Only the first search produced a count.

title: Can the helper report a total?

beats.say: How many newlines are in these three files? On Linux, this shell helper checks the directory size with disk usage. Find selects the JSONL files and word count reads each through standard input. That gives us one number per file.
The second filename has a space. The third has a newline. Read the two lines inside that last slot as one name. Find passes each complete name to the shell as one argument.
The first file has three newlines. The second has two. The third has one. That makes six. Run it again with the second file unreadable. Should the helper print the three it counted so far?

Stop before summing. The failed read ends this batch. Find returns failure and the helper returns before it prints a total. If the directory itself is missing, the disk usage check stops the helper before the first read. Back to the unreadable file.

Watch what happens when we put its read inside a local declaration. Bash returns zero because it declared the variable. Now declare the variable on its own line. The assignment returns one for the failed read, so the helper returns one too.

Grep looks for the word restored. The file is missing, so the error goes to standard error. The pipe carries only standard output. Word count receives an empty stream. It prints zero and exits successfully. Which status will Bash give the caller?

The pipeline returns zero. By default Bash takes the last command’s status, and word count succeeded. Turn on pipefail and run the same command. Word count still prints zero. This time Bash returns two, the error from grep.

Now there are three stages. Read the statuses from the right. Bash waits for the foreground pipeline to finish. With pipefail, skip over zeros and take the first nonzero status you reach. Here the pipeline reports seven. If every stage succeeds, you get zero.
An ordinary pipe carries standard output. Standard error stays separate unless you redirect it. Save the status before another command replaces it.

With nounset, lowercase u, expanding an unset variable directly raises an error. Give that variable an explicit default and Bash can use the fallback. Now look at the function on the left. It uses errexit, lowercase e. That option exits on many unhandled failures.
Here an if statement tests the function. What happens after the false command inside it?

The function prints continued. That successful print makes the function return zero, so the caller prints accepted. Run it again with an explicit return at the failed command. Now both prints are skipped. The function returns one.
When you test grep, handle status one as a search with no matches and a read error as a failure.

Save this Bash script on the server and make it executable. Before the loop starts, install its TERM trap. The on-term function writes a final log line and exits with zero. Run the script from the project root. Each time the scorer passes, the loop writes the next check number. If the scorer fails, the loop exits with that status.

Suppose you want the terminal back tomorrow. Start the loop in a named tmux session. Now SSH disconnects. Watch the terminal log. It gains another completed check while you’re away. Reattach to the named session and you’re back at the same running command.

For a separate, noninteractive run, create the runs directory. Start the same loop with nohup so it ignores hangup. Redirect both output streams to the log and take input from the null device. The trailing ampersand backgrounds the command. Save its process ID in this shell.

We’ll keep that shell open. For an interactive terminal, choose tmux. Inside the session, nice asks to increase the loop’s niceness by ten. Under normal scheduling it generally gets a smaller CPU share when other jobs compete. GPU memory, reboots and scheduler stops are separate concerns.

Return to the shell that started the background loop. It saved the child’s process ID. Inspect the owner, process ID, start time and command. For a GPU job, the NVIDIA tool can show memory use and list candidate processes to inspect.
Our shell loop runs a CPU scorer. If a run never starts, check that the input is readable and the runner executable. For this running job, first confirm you have permission to stop it.

Send TERM to the loop. Give it up to ten seconds to finish. Check the PID before each one-second sleep. The Bash trap calls on-term. That function writes its final log line and exits with zero. The PID disappears. Check once more after the loop.
If the PID is still present, report it and recheck its identity. Here the child has exited. Use wait in the launching shell and save the child's status immediately. This child returned zero.
Look up that number again. The existence check succeeds. Read the new process listing beside the original. The owner and number match. Would you send a stronger signal now?

Leave the backup job running. Its start time is later and its command is different. A zero signal checks existence and permission. The number can be reused. Consider a forced stop only for the same authorized job after a grace period and an identity check.
A forced stop gives its cleanup handler no chance to run.

title: Which Python will the clone run?

beats.say: We’ve identified the right process. Now consider the teammate starting it. The clone receives the setup script. Build a new virtual environment there, select its Python, and verify the version. This scorer uses the standard library. Its requirements file has no packages to install.
If that changes, the checkout will need a complete lock or fully pinned and hashed requirements.

Look at the tracked template. It carries a name with an empty value. Leave it blank. Suppose an application reads its key from a local dot env file. To create that file, copy the template. Set the key in the ignored copy. This scorer needs no key.
Model weights can have a different handoff. Git L F S records a pointer and fetches separate bytes. A run that uses those weights must check that the bytes arrived.

title: Can the clone start its scorer?

beats.say: Follow the selected interpreter into a new virtual environment. A version manager can read dot python version. The file is a hint. Here, python three creates the environment. The setup script activates it and checks that its Python is at least three point twelve. It exports the environment’s interpreter so the scorer uses that copy.
Virtual environments can contain absolute paths. That’s why we rebuild them at the destination.

If this scorer needs packages later, we’ll need their dependencies too. A uv project records them in its lockfile alongside the project declaration. Sync locked refuses an out-of-date lock. With pip, pin and hash all direct and transitive requirements and include hashes for the artifacts you accept.
Run pip install with hash checking in the activated environment. Either choice leaves the operating system, driver and system libraries to the host.

Say the caller exports a Python path that does not exist. The missing-interpreter trial returns one in the helper. The sourced file preserves that failure through cleanup. Now source returns one to the calling shell. With errexit off, which command skips the evaluation runner?

The two ampersands skip the runner when setup fails. A semicolon starts the runner anyway. Here it reports the missing interpreter before it can score a row. Repair setup before evaluating. The setup script leaves the ignored environment file unread.
Sourcing it would execute its contents as shell code. This scorer needs no secret.

Suppose the driver and container expose these three GPUs. The NVIDIA listing shows the driver’s view. The cards show CUDA’s device numbers before masking. Start a fresh process with the visibility list on screen. Which original CUDA device becomes application device zero?
Read the list from the left. Application zero maps to original CUDA device two. The next entry is zero, so application one maps to original CUDA device zero. The host still has all three devices.
Try a fresh process with the mask set to an empty string. How many devices can the application see now?

No CUDA devices are visible to this process. The host still has its three GPUs. Unset the variable in another fresh process and the runtime’s available devices are normally unmasked. Record the mask, driver listing, interpreter and framework probe together. A missing container device, incompatible driver or missing Python package needs its own diagnosis.

title: What did Git LFS put in the checkout?

beats.say: Suppose a larger model belongs under version control. Git L F S keeps a small pointer in Git. We’ll use eight example bytes so you can inspect the whole object. The pointer names its digest and size. If the checkout still contains pointer text, can the model loader read those eight bytes yet?

It needs the payload. With L F S installed and the object available on the server, pull it into the checkout. Fetch the required object and check it arrived. Its length and digest identify these eight bytes.
The article’s skeleton commit stages only the ignore rules and attributes. If L F S is unavailable, leave the weights out of the commit. Our three saved predictions run without them.

Try adding the required model to a repository that already tracks both configuration files. Its ignore file lists the model extension. Ask Git L F S to track that extension. It writes one rule to the attributes file. The model is still ignored. Remove the conflicting ignore pattern, then stage all three paths together.

Read the staged changes. Both configuration files are modified. The new model enters the index as a pointer. Commit all three changes together. For changing datasets, a versioned manifest can point to external storage. Record each required nonsecret input in the setup instructions.

Return to the opening terminals. The setup files are already staged. Stage the original three requests, then commit the fixture and setup. Make a new temporary directory. In a checking subshell with errexit enabled, clone into it. The shell is still in the old directory.
Change into the clone and stop if that fails. Ask Git to list the tracked path. Its name comes back from the index. Can the runner open it?

Install the tracked hook in this clone. Suppose its selected Python is missing. Run the guarded source command inside the checking subshell. If activation fails, can the later Git status command make this check look successful?

Setup returns one. The explicit exit ends the checking subshell right there. The parent shell has errexit off. It immediately saves the status and prints one. The scorer and Git status both stayed idle.

Restore the selected Python. Repeat the check in a fresh clone and install the hook there. Source the activation script. It builds a local environment and setup verifies its version. Run the repository command under errexit. What should the clone print?
Two matches in three requests, zero point six six seven. The scorer passed. Ask Git for its short status. It prints nothing here, even with the ignored environment on disk.

As soon as the subshell finishes, save its status in the parent shell. The next command sets its own status. Print the saved value. For this passing run, it is zero. Both checkouts used the tools, operating system and driver on this host.
Run the check on your teammate’s machine to see whether their setup reproduces the score.

Here’s a fresh file with seven requests. Read the expected answers and the saved predictions. Trim the spaces and convert each label to lowercase. Count the matches yourself. Would the two-thirds gate open?

The last two requests both predict escalated. Their expected answers differ from that word. Seven requests put the required mark at fourteen. Five matches put us at fifteen. It passes. Five sevenths prints as zero point seven one four. Keep your eye on the mark for those five matches.

Append a wrong eighth request and stage that file. Now remove the extra row only in the working copy. The hook again reads five matches in seven and passes. You make a plain commit. Will the fresh clone pass? Which request tells you?

Follow the selected file into the new clone. Request two hundred eight came with it. The extra miss moves the required mark past the five matches. Fifteen is below sixteen. The clone scores five eighths, or zero point six two five, and the gate fails. Which copy needs to change?

Stage the removal of the trial request. Check the staged difference. There’s the deletion of request two hundred eight. Record that change in a new commit. Rebuild from that commit in another empty directory. Install the hook, activate the environment, and run the scorer. The clone passes.

Your teammate can check out this commit and test the same seven requests. To share the result, give them the commit and the command that earned it. The next lesson uses a container to specify more of the environment.
